seo.title: Karmic tail 3 22 19 compatibility: from the garden into the sun
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 22 19 compatibility: The Empress at the entry, The Fool in the middle, The Sun as the main task, read through the Song of Songs, with an example.

title: Karmic tail 3-22-19 in compatibility: out of the enclosed garden into the sun
short: The Song of Songs has a verse that holds this whole tail. A young woman asks not to be stared at: "Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother's children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept." In the next line she asks her beloved where he rests "at noon", "for why should I be as one that turneth aside", a stray among the flocks. The vineyard is The Empress, the sun is The Sun, the stray is The Fool. Karmic tail 3-22-19 in compatibility describes a couple whose task is to bring their love out of a closed garden into daylight and still keep a vineyard of one's own for each of them.

sections.h2: A book in which a couple speaks in two voices
paragraphs: The Song of Songs is eight short chapters, and almost all of it is a conversation between two people. The title itself is built like "Holy of Holies": a superlative, the finest of songs. She calls, he answers, and they describe each other in the same words: he tells her "thou hast doves' eyes", she says of him, "His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the rivers of waters". Out of such echoes a couple's common language grows. On the compatibility chart the common language sits on the same point as the entry to the task.

There is no running plot in the book, only scenes. But read in order, they follow the order of this tail. The opening has vineyards, "a garden inclosed" and a mother's house. The middle has a roe leaping on the mountains, night searches through the city and a door opened too late. The ending has the sun, a seal upon the heart and the line "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me", which answers the complaint of the first chapter.

The speakers are a woman and a man, but the roles of the tail are not divided by sex. In a living couple either of the two can be the one who calls "Rise up… and come away" and the one who did not open the door in time.

The first clue lies in the elements. Benebell Wen gives each card an element: for her The Empress is governed by Earth, The Fool by Air, The Sun by Fire. The Song of Songs follows the same order. First comes earth bearing fruit behind a fence: "A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed." Then air, and no stranger opens the garden: the bride calls the wind herself. "Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out." At the end comes fire: "the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame. Many waters cannot quench love".

For a couple this is a route through three states. At first love can be touched: home, food, things, a shared household. Then it cannot be held: it is on the road, in change, in the wind. At the end it shines and warms, and if there is too much fire, it burns. Wen makes the centre of this couple a fire card too: Strength, she writes, is governed by Fire. The atmosphere and the main task burn with one flame.

The second clue lies in Waite's divinatory lists. Under The Empress he has "the unknown, clandestine". Under The Fool, "bewrayment", an old word usually glossed as the revealing of a secret. The Sun he calls direct light, "the antithesis of the reflected light". Secret, disclosure, daylight: the same road the couple of the Song of Songs walks.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: honey and milk under the tongue
paragraphs: "Thy lips, O my spouse, drop as the honeycomb: honey and milk are under thy tongue". What lies under this couple's tongue is food, garden and harvest. The love talk of the book is rural through and through: vineyards, pomegranates, fig trees, lilies, spikenard and saffron. Love here is measured in fruit, not in vows.

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together and where their shared road begins. With The Empress it is a wish for fullness. The two quickly start speaking the language of care: who cooked what, what to buy for the house, what the kitchen will look like, where to go out of town at the weekend. Lisovskaya sums up the Three in three words, fertility, abundance and growth, and holds that the couple met for the sake of the area where these will grow. For some it is a family and a shared table, for others a business that lifts both of them within a couple of years, for others a house out of town instead of a rented flat. The Song of Songs has a scene that reads like the programme of such a union: "Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field; let us lodge in the villages. Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see if the vine flourish… which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved." To go out into the field, see what has blossomed and show what has been saved: this is what Empress love looks like.

Wen writes that The Empress has "an incredible gift for harnessing interpersonal relationships to yield success and harmony". Couples like this know how to make a home that guests are drawn to, and a shared venture that grows faster than either partner's would alone.

But the entry to the task stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish can turn into resistance. The garden in the book is beautiful and locked. The heroine brings her beloved not to a place of her own but "into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me", and in the eighth chapter she dreams again of bringing him into her mother's house. Her work was decided by her brothers: "they made me the keeper of the vineyards". The first of The Empress's tasks for a couple, in Lisovskaya's list, is getting out from under the influence of the mother and the wider family. In real life this is a couple whose every holiday is spent at the parents', and whose renovation is first cleared with the elders. Or a couple where one feeds and settles the other so diligently that the other has no reason to get up from the cushions, and a few years later one has grown and the other has not.

One more line is about small things: "Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes." A vineyard in blossom is spoiled not by bears but by fox cubs. It is the same with this couple: the union is rarely broken by a great misfortune; it is worn down by small things nobody mentioned. "Fine, I'll do it myself", a forgotten promise, a present instead of a conversation. Wen describes the reversed Empress as "a sense of emptiness and no production after much work and effort". That is how a home feels where much work was done and no harvest is in sight.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a roe behind the wall
paragraphs: "The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills. My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice." The Fool of the Song of Songs stands right behind the garden fence. And he calls: "Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away. For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone".

In Lisovskaya's book the middle of the task has no meaning of its own; it is an "addition" to the main task. On the site we read it like this: how the couple lives the road from the wish of the entry to the main task. For this couple the road goes through The Fool, which means in leaps. The two may move to another city half a year after meeting, drop a secure job for a shared venture, start from zero after a failure and find a way out where others would sit down to grieve. On the bright side Lisovskaya sees in The Fool a trust that grows into freedom: the two live like best friends and do not cling to things. Such a couple is bored standing still, and it is movement that takes it out of the locked garden.

For Wen, The Fool is a card of a fork in the road: the next step "could either send the Seeker flying into the air over that cliff with impressive accomplishment or falling down hard from naïveté". Every leap this couple makes is such a fork. How it ends is more often decided not by the leap itself but by whether the two jump together.

The price of the leaps is in the most recognisable scene of the book. At night he knocks: "Open to me… for my head is filled with dew". She has already gone to bed: "I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?" She gets up and opens, "but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone". One came with an impulse when the other had settled into comfort; when the second was ready, the first was gone. Lisovskaya describes this shadow of The Fool precisely: starting is easy, and trouble comes as soon as it is time for serious steps. In daily life it is the endless "let's do it later", and the question "what are we to each other" hangs in the air for years. One has found a flat in another city, the other says "not now". One is ready for a wedding while the other is in a phase of freedom, and a year later it is the other way round.

After the unopened door the heroine goes looking for her beloved through the city at night, asks the watchmen, and then begs everyone she meets: "if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love." The secret of the garden goes out into the street. This is the "bewrayment" from The Fool's list: the disclosure without which there is no reaching The Sun. The middle of the tail drags what was hidden into the light, awkwardly, at night, in front of strangers, but it does drag it out.

The numbers show something odd about this couple's Fool. It is always the sum of the two personal tail middles, exactly 22 with no reduction, and neither partner has The Fool in their own tail, not in a single couple of this kind. The roe lives in neither of the two houses; it leaps between them. And in 64% of such couples the personal middles are The Sun (19) for one partner and The Empress (3) for the other. The road from the garden into the sun is literally built from one partner's garden and the other's sun.

sections.h2: Main task: the sun that looks
paragraphs: Back to the verse where it all began: "Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me". The Hebrew verb in this verse means "to catch sight of, look on", and the King James Bible keeps that sense: the sun has looked at her. In the Song of Songs the sun is a gaze. That is why this couple's main task is about how the two look at each other and how they are seen.

Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through its shadow: what the two cannot manage and what they have to learn. For The Sun this shadow is scorching light, and its first form is named in the same verse. The heroine kept other people's vineyards and neglected her own. In a couple this is the one whose talent spends years working for the shared home, for the other's career, for the family business, while their own stands idle. Lisovskaya calls this a failure to realise oneself and taking credit for the partner's victories. It is easy to spot by the pronouns: "we got the PhD", "I'm the one who pulled him through", "our success", in which nobody remembers any more whose it was.

The second form is light that presses down. In the sixth chapter they say of the heroine: "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?" Clear and terrible in one line. Admiration easily becomes a demand: "you can do better", "look how others manage", "I was counting on you". Lisovskaya puts this into the shadow of The Sun: expectations higher than the person, comparisons, and control over whom the partner sees and where they grow. Wen writes that The Sun "could suggest a power couple" and that it is "a card about dominance and captivating the attention and respect of others". For two people with Strength in the centre and The Sun as their task this is a trap: two strong people under one sky start arguing over whose light comes first.

The third form is love that may not go out into the street. "O that thou wert as my brother… when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised." All the tenderness stays at home, at night, behind the wall, and in public there is restraint. Lisovskaya also counts an inability to talk about problems and holding feelings back among the tasks of The Sun. The couple lives beautifully in its own garden, but every difficult conversation is put off until night, and at night until tomorrow.

There is also the opposite extreme: light for show. The chorus in the book cries: "Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee", and the answer comes: "What will ye see in the Shulamite?" A sunny couple easily starts living for an audience: beautiful photographs, the right image, a compulsory brightness that tires sooner than love does.

On the bright side of The Sun, for Lisovskaya, each partner succeeds in their own work, and the growth of one pushes the growth of the other. The book has one line for this: "his banner over me was love". What flies over this couple should be love, not status, not a ranking and not a score of who pulled whom through.

If control in a couple turns into fear or threat, it is no longer a matter for reading cards. Real help is needed: a psychologist, close friends and family, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

The numbers hold this task as precisely as they hold the entry. The couple's Sun is always the exact sum of the two personal karmic tasks, with no reduction. In 64% of such couples it is The Chariot (7) of one partner and The Hanged Man (12) of the other: one rushes ahead, the other knows how to wait, and together they make 19.

sections.h2: Centre of the couple: "love is strong as death"
paragraphs: The centre of a couple is its atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. Tail 3-22-19 has only one centre: 11, Strength, in 100% of such couples. And the Song of Songs has the most famous line in the book for it: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death". In the Latin Vulgate: fortis est ut mors dilectio. Waite calls this card "Strength, or Fortitude", and in his divinatory list simply "Fortitude", from the same Latin fortis. The atmosphere of this couple is a love that holds fast.

The same line gives the shadow at once: "jealousy is cruel as the grave". The shadow of Strength in a couple shows up as an argument in which both are right and neither gives way: for Lisovskaya this is a struggle for leadership in which each has their own truth. On the bright side she describes Strength as a couple in which each senses keenly what the other needs, and tension goes not into a quarrel but into passion.

Three times the book repeats the same refrain: "I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please." The Hebrew says simply "love" (ahavah), not "my love": do not wake love until it wants to wake. This is the formula of Strength at its best. Wen writes that the card "is a reminder that the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence". For a couple with The Fool in the middle this matters especially. A leap the other was dragged into by force turns into that same night of the unopened door.

Strength has its lion in the book as well. The bridegroom calls the bride: "Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse… look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards." Love comes down into the garden from the lions' dens.

And the last clue is in the first part of Waite's book. The highest degree of this virtue he calls "the state of Royal Fortitude, which is the state of a Tower of Ivory and a House of Gold". These are two titles of the Virgin Mary from the Litany of Loreto, and the tower of ivory came into the litany from the Song of Songs: "Thy neck is as a tower of ivory", in the Vulgate turris eburnea. Waite describes the highest form of this couple's centre card with an image from this couple's own book.

The image has a sequel. In 1837 Sainte-Beuve turned it into a phrase that is still in use: the poet Vigny, he wrote, "Comme en sa tour d'ivoire, avant midi, rentrait", "withdrew, as into his ivory tower, before noon" (our translation). So the Strength of this couple acquires a shadow: a fortress the two retreat into before noon, that is, before their Sun. A strong couple closed off from the world may never come out into the light.

sections.h2: Three cards in Waite: the banner, the morning and the open jaws
paragraphs: The Waite deck, drawn by Pamela Colman Smith, adds three details to the story.

On Waite's Sun card a naked child on a white horse displays "a red standard". The Song of Songs names the banner outright: "He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love." Describing the same card, Wen notes that its sun "has a face, somehow both stern and serene". It is the same doubleness as in "clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners".

Waite sets The Fool at the edge of a precipice and names the hour: it all happens "amidst the morning glory, in the keen air". The Fool is morning, The Sun is full day. The couple of the book keeps hours too. "Until the day break, and the shadows flee away", the roe leaps on the mountains. And the heroine's first question to her beloved is where he rests "at noon". The middle of this tail is dawn; the main task is noon.

On Waite's Strength card the woman is closing the lion's mouth. But in the first part of his book Waite adds a note: in the earlier form printed by Court de Gebelin "she is obviously opening it". The closing version, he says, "is better symbolically". A couple whose main task is to speak in daylight does well to remember that Strength once had two gestures: it can hold back the roar, and it can let the voice out.

sections.h2: The couple's values: from "he is mine" to "I am his"
paragraphs: "The couple's values" are the spiritual purpose, the road the two are to walk together. This tail has only two options there: The Lovers (6) in 63.4% of couples and The Devil (15) in 36.6%. Both cards are about belonging, and the Song of Songs has a ladder that shows the difference.

It is worth writing three lines one under another. Chapter two: "My beloved is mine, and I am his". Chapter six: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine". Chapter seven: "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me." At first "he is mine" comes first. Then "I am his". At the end the word "mine" disappears altogether, leaving "I am his, and he desires me".

Our reading: this is the road from The Devil to The Lovers. The Devil among the values is the temptation to hold love as property. Lisovskaya writes about attempts to keep a partner by closeness, money or status, and sums up the card in the phrase "nobody belongs to anybody". The book answers in chapter eight: "if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned." All the riches of The Empress are not enough to buy what is given only by choice. The Lovers are that choice, repeated in daylight.

The word "desire" in chapter seven (teshuqah) occurs only three times in the Bible. The first time is in Genesis, where it stands next to power: "and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee." The biblical scholar Phyllis Trible, in God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (1978, the chapter "Love's Lyric Redeemed"), reads the line of the Song as an answer to those words: the desire remains, the rule is gone. For a couple with The Devil among its values this is the very work: keep the attraction and remove the power.

sections.h2: The strong version: a vineyard of one's own for each
paragraphs: The last chapter of the Song of Songs gathers the way out of this tail into four movements.

First the brothers again decide for their sister: "If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she be a door, we will inclose her with boards of cedar." And for the first time she answers for herself: "I am a wall… then was I in his eyes as one that found favour." Where the King James has "favour", the Hebrew word is shalom, peace. The Empress no longer lives by the family's plan: the two decide for themselves where they have a wall and where a door.

Then the vineyard. Solomon lets out his vineyard to keepers for a thousand pieces of silver. The heroine replies: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me". The complaint of the first chapter, "mine own vineyard have I not kept", is closed. This is The Sun at its best: each has their own work, their own harvest and their own joy, and instead of competing they warm the shared home.

Then the voice. "Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it." In the second chapter the heroine was hiding "in the clefts of the rock", and her beloved asked, "let me hear thy voice". By the end everyone hears her voice, and he asks to hear it too. Love has come out into the light, and its main listener has stayed close.

And the last line of the book: "Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices." In chapter two the word was "turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe", that is, come back. In chapter eight it is a different verb, which the King James softens to "make haste" and which in Hebrew means "flee". The book ends not with a lock but with freedom, and that freedom comes after the seal upon the heart. The Fool in the strong version of the tail is trust: the two let each other go because they are not afraid of losing each other.
In the everyday life of a couple with tail 3-22-19 it looks like this:

ul: **A vineyard of one's own for each.** One's own work, money and friends next to the shared garden. Lisovskaya plainly advises such couples to find self-realisation separately and to learn to make decisions alone.
**Catch the little foxes while the vine is in blossom.** Mention a small irritation the same day, while it is still small.
**Leap by agreement.** Before a big step, ask whether the other is "dressed", and name a date instead of "later". Think about responsibility before the leap, not after it.
**Call victories by their names.** Say out loud whose success it is, give thanks, and do not turn it into "ours" without asking.
**Love in the street too.** Tenderness, plans and difficult conversations belong not only to the night and not only to the home. But not to the chorus that cries "return, return" either.
**Do not wake love by force.** Do not drag the other into a decision they have not grown into yet.
**Freedom with a seal.** Let the other go without checking up, on a trip, to friends, into their own work, and bear temporary separations calmly.

sections.h2: How tail 3-22-19 comes about: a worked example
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. A couple's tail is not recalculated from its outer numbers: the couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles. Example: the couple born 05.12.1975 and 05.07.1975. The first partner has the personal tail 18-3-12 and centre 6, the second has 12-19-7 and centre 5.

This couple's middle is put together exactly as described above: The Empress from one partner's personal tail and The Sun from the other's give The Fool. The Sun appears twice more in this couple's matrix. On the point What to create together (12 + 7 = 19), where it occurs in only 4.1% of couples with this tail. And on the Way into money (10 + 9 = 19), in 4.9%. So for this couple the main task and the reason they met coincide. Strength repeats too: in the centre and on the point What fills (17 + 12 = 29 → 11), which happens in 6.8% of these couples. By Lisovskaya's rule, repeated energies can be added: 11 + 11 = 22, which gives The Fool, already standing in the middle of the tail. The couple's values are 6, The Lovers.
The other numbers describe all couples with this tail at once. They come from running every date since 1900 through the site's engine:

ul: tail 3-22-19 occurs in roughly one couple in 83 (1.204%), 29th place among the 97 couple tails;
the couple's entry to the task is always the sum 30: 12 + 18 (78%) or 21 + 9 (22%), and neither partner has The Empress on their own personal entry;
the middle is always exactly 22 and the main task always exactly 19, with no reduction;

neither partner ever has The Fool in their personal tail; The Empress is in one partner's tail in 74.7% of couples, The Sun in 64%; in 25.3% of couples none of the three cards appears in the personal tails, and the tail is formed entirely between two people;
the centre is Strength in 100%; from the personal centres it adds up as 5 + 6 (74.7%), 3 + 8 (22.3%) or 18 + 11 (3%);
the values are The Lovers (63.4%) or The Devil (36.6%).

paragraphs: There is no couple tail made of the same numbers in a different order: neither 3-19-22 nor 22-3-19 nor any other permutation occurs for couples. The triple 3-22-19 does, however, occur as a personal karmic tail, for 1,038 dates since 1900. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article about it.

ul: **Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** The two want a fruitful life: a home and a garden of their own, a full table, care that can be tasted. The same wish keeps them in comfort and in the parental home, where nobody ever leaves.

**Middle of the task — 22, The Fool.** The road goes in leaps: moves, fresh starts from zero, a sudden "let's go", freedom and play. The price is missed timing: one calls the other outside when the other is not ready yet.

**Main task — 19, The Sun.** Learning to live in view and in truth: saying hard things out loud, being glad of the other's success without taking it over, growing something of one's own for each. The shadow of The Sun is a scorching gaze: control, inflated expectations, comparisons and somebody's abandoned vineyard.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 3-22-19 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that starts from a wish for a full, fruitful life (The Empress), moves towards its goal through leaps and changes (The Fool) and learns the main thing, which is to live in daylight: to talk about hard things, to be glad of the other's success and to keep work of one's own for each (The Sun).

faq.q: How does a couple get tail 3 22 19?
faq.a: Each point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. In such couples the entry to the task always gives 30 → 3, the middle exactly 22 and the main task exactly 19. Most often (64%) the tail is made from the personal tails 12-19-7 and 18-3-12.

faq.q: How is couple tail 3-22-19 different from personal tail 3-22-19?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date and describes one person's task, with its own roles for the points. A couple's tail is added up from two matrices and speaks of what the two have to learn together. The same numbers do not make these readings interchangeable.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 3, 22 and 19 a couple can only get the order 3-22-19: permutations such as 3-19-22 or 19-22-3 do not occur in the compatibility matrix.

faq.q: Does tail 3-22-19 predict what will happen to a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail is a symbolic map of a task, not a forecast of events and not a verdict on the union. It shows where the couple's difficulties repeat and which version of the story is stronger, and the choice belongs to the two of them.

That talent spends years working for the shared home or the other's career, and later the success sounds like "we got the PhD" or "I'm the one who pulled him through". The second is light that presses down. The heroine is called "clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners", and admiration easily turns into a demand, the familiar "could do better". Wen writes that The Sun "could suggest a power couple", and for two people with Strength in the centre this is a trap: **two strong people under one sky argue over whose light comes first.** The third is love that may not go out into the street: "when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised." Tenderness stays at home, behind the wall, and a difficult conversation is put off until night, and at night until tomorrow.

If control in a couple turns into fear or threat, it is no longer a matter for reading cards: real help is needed, a psychologist, close friends and family, and in danger a local emergency number or crisis line.

The centre of every such couple is Strength, and the book gives it its most famous line: "love is strong as death", in the Vulgate fortis est ut mors dilectio. Waite calls the card Fortitude, from the same fortis. The same line holds its shadow: "jealousy is cruel as the grave". And the refrain repeated three times gives its bright side: the Hebrew says "love", not "my love", so it reads as "do not wake love until it wants to wake". A leap the other was dragged into by force ends in a night with an unopened door.

Waite describes the highest Fortitude as "a Tower of Ivory", an image that came from the same Song of Songs. And in 1837 Sainte-Beuve wrote of a poet who "withdrew, as into his ivory tower, before noon". That is the shadow of the centre: a strong couple can retreat into its fortress before noon, that is, before its Sun.

report.h3: My vineyard, which is mine, is before me

report: The last chapter of the book gathers the way out. The brothers once more decide for their sister, and for the first time she answers for herself: "I am a wall". Solomon lets out his vineyard to keepers for a thousand pieces of silver, and the heroine says: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me". The complaint of the first chapter is closed: **each has their own work and their own harvest, and both warm the shared home.** Her beloved asks to hear the voice that everyone already hears. And the last line of the book is not a lock but freedom: "Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe". That freedom comes after the seal upon the heart.

The book also shows the ladder of the couple's values: "My beloved is mine", then "I am my beloved's", then "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me". The word "mine" disappears. In our reading this is the road from The Devil to The Lovers: a love that "all the substance of his house" cannot buy is held by choice, not by ownership.

In practice this means a vineyard of one's own for each next to the shared garden, little foxes caught the same day, leaps by agreement with a date instead of "later", victories called by their names, tenderness and difficult conversations not only at night, and freedom without checking up.
